title: Ten healed, one returned (Luke 17:11–19)
hook: ten lepers healed; only a Samaritan comes back to say thank you

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mustard seed of faith, enough to move a tree. Your line was increase our faith.

Between Samaria and Galilee, at the edge of a village, ten men stand at a distance. They have to. They have leprosy, the Bible's word for skin diseases that made a person unclean, and the law said they must live apart: no home, no work, no family's touch. At least one, we'll learn, is a Samaritan. Trouble has put them all on the same road. They see Jesus coming, and they don't come closer. They lift up their voices.

In the King James Bible they cry: "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us." He doesn't touch them or say be healed. He says: "Go shew yourselves unto the priests." The law required a priest to confirm someone had recovered. But they haven't, yet. They have to start walking while still sick. "And it came to pass, that, as they went, they were cleansed." Then the turn: "And one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, and with a loud voice glorified God, And fell down on his face at his feet, giving him thanks: and he was a Samaritan." The same loud voice he'd used to beg, now used to praise. Giving thanks, in Greek, is eucharisteo. Eu, good; charis, grace or gift. It's where the word Eucharist comes from, the name Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Anglicans and others use for communion, the great thanksgiving. Jesus asks: "Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine?" To be fair, the nine were doing what they were told, heading to the priests. Luke never calls them ungrateful. But only one turned around and came back first. Jesus calls him "this stranger," a foreigner. The outsider is the one who sees the gift. Then: "Arise, go thy way: thy faith hath made thee whole." All ten were cleansed. Some readers notice that only this one hears he's been made whole. The healing reached his skin. The thanks reached further.
screen: then, large: `THY FAITH HATH MADE THEE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last year to one good thing you received and walked on from: a recovery, a favor, someone who stood by you when they didn't have to. Picture yourself turning around on the road, and find the words you'd say to them. If you pray, turn back to God with the same thanks.
Eucharisteo, Greek for giving thanks, good grace: what the healed Samaritan did when he turned back, and the root of the word Eucharist.
Your line: where are the nine? One came back, and heard he'd been made whole. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Anglicans, Lutherans and others call communion the Eucharist, the thanksgiving; in the United States, some churches read the story of the ten lepers around Thanksgiving.

chat.says: Why does Jesus ask where the nine are? Weren't they just doing what he told them?
options: They were, and Luke never calls them ungrateful; but only one turned back to give thanks.
They weren't; the nine refused to go to the priests and stayed where they were.
Because the nine were never actually healed; only the Samaritan was cleansed.
chat.meaning: All ten were cleansed on the way to the priests. Only the Samaritan turned back, giving thanks, and heard: thy faith hath made thee whole.

eucharisteo.meaning: Greek for giving thanks: eu, good, and charis, grace

Eucharist.meaning: communion, named for the great thanksgiving

Samaritan.meaning: someone from Samaria; in this story, the outsider

leprosy.meaning: the Bible's word for skin diseases that made someone unclean

notes: The index word is 'eucharisteo' (transliteration, unaccented); kept exactly. Luke 17:16 uses the participle εὐχαριστῶν.
'Mixed group, Jews and at least one Samaritan': the text names only the one Samaritan; the others' identity is inferred. Confirm phrasing.
Biblical 'leprosy' covering various skin diseases: standard. Confirm.
Reading 'made whole' (σέσωκεν, 'saved') as something more than the nine's cleansing is a common interpretation, presented as 'many readers notice'.
Thanksgiving-season reading in US churches: common in lectionaries (e.g. Year C). Confirm.
